analysis.one_liner: Restores workers' ability to prove age discrimination by letting them show age was one motivating factor, not the sole cause.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by a bipartisan group of four senators, never received a hearing or vote in the Senate and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2009 the Supreme Court ruled in Gross v. FBL Financial that workers claiming age discrimination must prove age was the deciding reason for an adverse job action — a much harder standard than for race or sex discrimination. This bill would overturn that ruling: a worker would win by showing age was a "motivating factor," even if other factors also mattered. It would apply the same standard to disability discrimination claims. If an employer proved it would have made the same decision anyway, the worker could get a court ruling but no money damages.
analysis.who_benefits: Older workers (and, under the extended provisions, disability discrimination claimants) who believe they were fired, demoted, or passed over partly because of their age. They would no longer have to prove age was the sole reason for the decision — only that it was a motivating factor — and could rely on any admissible evidence. Workers in mixed-motive cases who can prove discrimination but not sole causation would at least get a court declaration and attorney's fees where the employer shows the same decision would have been made anyway.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes that age discrimination is proven when age was a 'motivating factor' in an employment decision, even if other factors also played a role, reversing the Supreme Court's Gross v. FBL Financial requirement that age be the sole 'but-for' cause.
Allows workers to use any type of admissible evidence, and rejects the requirement that age be the sole cause of the adverse decision.
Extends the same motivating-factor standard to discrimination claims based on race, sex, national origin, and disability under Title VII, the ADA, and the Rehabilitation Act.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would face a lower bar for age and disability discrimination lawsuits and more exposure to claims where multiple factors influenced a decision. The cost is litigation risk and settlements; the bill's compromise on same-decision cases limits damages in some of them.

drawbacks.text: Even under the bill, a worker who proves age was a motivating factor gets no money damages if the employer shows it would have made the same decision anyway — relief is limited to a court declaration and injunction in that case.
The bill would apply to all claims pending on or after enactment, exposing employers to new litigation over decisions already made under the stricter standard.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—restoring a realistic path to court for older, disabled, and other discriminated-against workers after a Supreme Court decision made such claims nearly impossible to win—is substantial and the costs modest. The bill itself contains the strongest compromise: where an employer proves it would have made the same decision anyway, victims get no money damages, only a court declaration. The main drawback is that the motivating-factor standard could still expose employers to more litigation over decisions that involved multiple considerations, and the bill would apply retroactively to pending claims. On balance it is a targeted fix to a proof standard, not a sweeping expansion of liability.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced with bipartisan sponsorship in March 2021, the bill was sent to the Senate health and labor committee and sat there until the Congress ended, with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 22, 2021 and read twice before being referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
The committee took no further action on the bill; it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
The bill's only recorded actions are its introduction and referral; it died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers accused of age discrimination are better off: the stricter Gross proof standard remains in force, so older workers still face a much heavier burden to win these cases.

for.name: Sen. Robert Casey Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led the effort to restore the motivating-factor standard for age discrimination claims.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor, giving the bill bipartisan leadership-level backing.

for.name: 3 of 50 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (including the two original Republican cosponsors).

for.name: 2 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill beyond the original Democratic sponsors.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; no bill can reach a vote without the majority leader scheduling one.

sides.party_line_note: Support was genuinely bipartisan — two of the four original sponsors were Republicans — but the bill died without any recorded vote, so the chamber's actual position was never tested.

industries.note: Would face easier age, disability, and retaliation discrimination lawsuits, with a lower burden of proof for workers and no cap change on damages where age truly mattered. The bill's compromise limits damages where the same decision would have been made anyway.
Would regain a practical ability to win age discrimination cases after the Gross decision made such claims very hard to prove.
